extracted.intended_audience: registrants (public companies), GHG emissions attestation providers, independent auditors, audit committees, and their legal/accounting advisors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and final-rule text regarding requirements for GHG emissions disclosures and the providers who attest to those disclosures, including eligibility, experience, independence, quality control, accreditation, exhibit and liability treatment, and related procedural requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference to attestation standards for 'significant experience'
rubrics_metrics.description: In the definition of 'significant experience' in the final rules, the prior reference to 'professional standards' is replaced with a reference to 'attestation standards' to make clear that the standards referenced in Item 1506(b)(1)(i) are the attestation standards that meet the requirements of Item 1506(a). See 17 CFR 229.1506(b)(1)(i).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This clarifies that 'significant experience' means experience under attestation standards (i.e., standards that meet Item 1506(a)), not some broader or different set of professional standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility of attestation providers (PCAOB-registered vs non-accounting firms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters urged that eligible attestation providers should not be limited to only PCAOB-registered audit firms and that non-accounting firms may provide assurance if they meet quality standards; others recommended requiring PCAOB-regulated entities because they are subject to oversight and inspection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Letters cited trade groups and commenters arguing both for broader eligibility to encourage competition and for limiting to PCAOB-regulated entities to ensure oversight and investor protection. The final rules recognize these considerations and discuss oversight/inspection limitations of the PCAOB.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expertise/experience requirements for attestation providers
rubrics_metrics.description: Attestation providers should have 'experience' meaning proper technical knowledge and competencies in STEM fields related to the sources and sinks of GHG emissions and removals being quantified; commenters recommended clarity about what 'experience' means and cautioned against prescribing a fixed number of years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some commenters recommended specifying required qualifications as was done in S-K 1300 for 'qualified person'; others cautioned that prescribing years of experience may limit new businesses whose employees have long-term experience. The Commission acknowledges the need for clearer guidance on requisite experience and competencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence requirement modeled on Rule 2-01
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rules provide that a GHG emissions attestation provider is not independent if the provider is not, or a reasonable investor would conclude is not, capable of exercising objective and impartial judgment on all issues encompassed within the attestation engagement; modeled on Rule 2-01(b) and the factors in the introductory text to Rule 2-01.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission will consider factors similar to Rule 2-01 in determining independence. The final rules do not alter Rule 2-01 or its applicability to financial statement audits. The Office of the Chief Accountant staff is available to consult regarding independence requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality control system requirement (ISQC 1 or equivalent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Attestation engagements performed by practitioners should be carried out by firms that are subject to ISQC 1 or 'other professional requirements, or requirements in law or regulation, regarding the firm's responsibility for its system of quality control' that are at least as demanding as ISQC 1 (IAASB ISAE 3000.3(b) (Revised)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters noted that firms accredited by IAF members must have a fully functional quality control and management system. The Commission discussed potential minimum quality control requirements for providers not registered with the PCAOB or otherwise subject to independent oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accreditation to ISO 14065 / IAF MLA as a basis for provider requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Some commenters recommended requiring a GHG emissions attestation provider to be accredited to ISO 14065 or be a signatory to the International Accreditation Forum's Multilateral Recognition Arrangement (IAF MLA) to ensure appropriate rigor and consistency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ISO standards (ISO 14065, ISO 14066) address impartiality, competency, and communication and are used by many non-accountant GHG attestation providers. The document notes these standards as possible bases for provider evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of AICPA and PCAOB attestation standards only to CPAs
rubrics_metrics.description: AICPA and PCAOB attestation standards apply only in the context of engagements performed by certified public accountants; PCAOB AT section 101 and AICPA SSAE No. 18 state those sections apply when a CPA in the practice of public accounting issues an examination, review, or agreed-upon procedures report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinction means non-CPA providers performing attestation-like services may not be covered by those professional standards, raising questions about which standards apply to non-accountant providers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engagement partner competence and specialist involvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters recommended aligning expertise requirements with ISAE 3000, which among other provisions requires the engagement partner to have 'competence in assurance skills and techniques' and 'sufficient competence in the underlying subject matter' and to ensure appropriate engagement of specialists (e.g., 'Auditor-Engaged Specialist').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CFA Institute and others recommended that providers have policies and procedures to ensure personnel selected have qualifications necessary to fulfill responsibilities and engage specialists where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Financial wherewithal and litigation exposure of attestation providers
rubrics_metrics.description: Some commenters recommended that GHG emissions attestation providers have the financial wherewithal to withstand potential litigation arising from their attestation services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission discussed liability implications, including how amendments to Rule 436 affect section 11 exposure for limited assurance reports, but noted other remedies (e.g., securities fraud claims) remain available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of limited assurance reports under Rule 436 and section 11 liability
rubrics_metrics.description: Amendments to Rule 436 provide that a report by a GHG emissions attestation provider covering Scope 1, Scope 2, and/or Scope 3 emissions at a limited assurance level shall not be considered part of the registration statement prepared or certified by an expert, thereby changing the application of the consent and related requirements under section 7 and affecting section 11 liability considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This change eliminates the section 7 consent requirement for those limited assurance reports in registration statements, but the Commission notes that other remedies (e.g., Exchange Act Rule 10b-5) are unaffected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence may prohibit firms that also provide other services
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters noted that the independence requirement could prohibit registrants from using firms that are otherwise the most qualified to provide attestations because those firms also provide other services (e.g., audit or consulting) to the registrant or affiliates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some argued this may be excessive, particularly where independence standards (like Rule 2-01) were designed for financial audits and may not be fully appropriate for non-accountant providers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fees for GHG attestation engagements and influence risk
rubrics_metrics.description: There is concern that fees for GHG attestation engagements may be small compared to financial audit fees, creating a potential risk of undue influence from the financial audit team if the same firm performs both services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ERM CVS flagged experience that small attestation fees may raise influence risk despite professional codes of conduct and independence requirements. The rules note fees for attestation may be considered 'Audit-Related Fees' when the independent accountant who audits consolidated financial statements is also engaged for GHG attestation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledgement letter exhibit requirement for limited assurance
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rules require registrants obtaining assurance at a limited assurance level to file a letter from the GHG emissions attestation provider as an exhibit (Instruction to Item 1506 directing registrants to Item 601(b)(27) and Form 20-F Instructions as to Exhibits 18).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This requirement is modeled on analogous requirements for accountant letters and is intended to provide notice to the assurance provider while imposing less burden than a consent requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitable recognized control framework for management's evaluation of internal control
rubrics_metrics.description: The framework on which management's evaluation of the issuer's internal control over financial reporting is based must be a suitable, recognized control framework established by a body that has followed due-process procedures, including broad distribution for public comment (citing 17 CFR240.13a-15(c) and 240.15d-15(c)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission cites its prior rules that require an established due-process framework for control frameworks used in management evaluations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alignment with IAASB/ISAE standards for GHG assurance engagements
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters noted that many GHG attestation engagements are already carried out in accordance with IAASB standards (ISAE 3000/3410) and recommended closer alignment between the Commission's requirements and those IAASB standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission references IAASB ISAE 3000 (Revised) and ISAE 3410 (Assurance Engagements on Greenhouse Gas Statements) as relevant standards and discusses how provider requirements relate to these international standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality control and oversight for non-PCAOB providers
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters recommended that non-PCAOB attestation providers be subject to requirements or oversight (e.g., additional minimum quality control requirements, peer review, accreditation) because AICPA/PCAOB standards and PCAOB inspection jurisdiction apply only to CPAs and may not cover non-accountant providers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendations included developing regulations to build intellectual infrastructure (independence requirements, quality management systems, peer review inspections) for non-accounting providers and considering accreditation mechanisms (ISO 14065, IAF MLA).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical availability/scarcity of qualified attestation providers
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple commenters expressed concern that there is a limited number of qualified firms and experienced personnel to provide GHG attestation services, which could make compliance challenging and costly for companies, particularly smaller registrants, in the near term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission acknowledges commenters' concerns that shortage of providers and independence constraints (e.g., prohibiting consultants who prepared inventories from attesting) may create practical difficulties; some commenters argued these constraints should not preclude provider availability.
